summary: Examines how Fibre Channel over Ethernet and TRILL can work together. Both forward hop by hop over Ethernet and change MAC addresses at each hop, and the document discusses how to combine them in data center networks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two delivery systems both swap the address sticker at every stop. This looks at how they can share the same trucks.

questions: how do fcoe and trill work together
what is fcrb in data center networks
subtitle: Running Fibre Channel over Ethernet inside TRILL-routed data center networks.

tldr.problem: Data centers traditionally use Fibre Channel for storage traffic and Ethernet for everything else. FCoE bridges these, but how can it work in a TRILL-routed network that also routes hop-by-hop over Ethernet while modifying MAC addresses?
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes two approaches: treating the TRILL cloud as transparent Ethernet (Separate Cloud), or combining FCoE Forwarders with TRILL Routing Bridges (FCRB) into single switches that serve both storage and data traffic.
tldr.outcome: The FCRB approach allows data centers to consolidate infrastructure, using the same equipment and cabling for both storage and data traffic while maintaining the benefits of both protocols.

today: RFC 6847 is an informational document published independently to the RFC Series. It has not been obsoleted and remains current as a description of architecture for integrating FCoE and TRILL in data center networks.

sections.title: What Are FCoE and TRILL
sections.content:
Fibre Channel over Ethernet (FCoE) encapsulates native Fibre Channel storage traffic inside Ethernet frames. It lets servers and storage arrays communicate using FCoE Forwarders (FCFs), which are devices that forward storage traffic based on Fibre Channel addresses while modifying Ethernet MAC addresses at each hop.

TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) is a routing protocol for data centers. TRILL-enabled switches called Routing Bridges (RBridges) forward Ethernet traffic hop-by-hop to a destination, also modifying MAC addresses at each hop, and use TRILL encapsulation with their own routing header.

Both FCoE and TRILL forward traffic hop-by-hop over Ethernet and modify MAC addresses at each stop. Both are designed for data centers. The problem is that deploying them together requires separate infrastructure and equipment, raising costs.
sections.eli5: Fibre Channel moves storage data through Ethernet. TRILL routes everything through Ethernet. Both change address labels at every hop, which sounds similar but needs careful coordination.

sections.title: The Separate Cloud Approach
sections.content:
The simplest way to run FCoE over TRILL is the Separate Cloud approach. The TRILL cloud acts as a simple Ethernet LAN to FCoE devices. FCoE Forwarders and TRILL Routing Bridges are separate devices. FCoE traffic (both data and control frames) travels through the TRILL cloud as standard Ethernet.

This approach has drawbacks. It requires more physical equipment and more cabling. More importantly, traffic between two FCoE nodes usually has to traverse the TRILL cloud twice: from the source node to an FCF, then through the cloud again to the destination node. This doubles the number of hops and reduces efficiency. For data centers that value minimal hop counts and high efficiency, this is a significant limitation.

To prevent frame loss, switches in the TRILL cloud must implement Data Center Bridging (DCB) protocols for flow control and congestion notification.
sections.eli5: The simplest way: treat TRILL as just a plain Ethernet network and run FCoE over it. The problem is you need more equipment and messages bounce around twice.

sections.title: FCoE over RBridge (FCRB)
sections.content:
A better approach combines both functions in a single device called FCRB (FCoE-forwarder-over-RBridge). An FCRB is logically two independent entities: an FCoE Forwarder (FCF) and a Routing Bridge (RBridge). The FCF appears to the RBridge as a native Ethernet host connected to one of its ports.

The FCRB approach allows data centers to consolidate infrastructure. Servers can be connected to the same switches that handle both storage and data traffic. Traffic between two servers connected to the same Top-of-Rack (ToR) FCRB bypasses the wider network entirely, traveling directly through that switch as if it were an FCF.

More importantly, the FCRB approach allows networks where FCRBs are connected to one another through a TRILL cloud, and also supports hybrid networks where some nodes are FCRBs while others are plain RBridges. This flexibility enables cost-effective network design.
sections.eli5: Put both a Fibre Channel forwarder and a TRILL router in one box. Now the same switch handles storage and data, and nearby servers talk directly instead of bouncing messages around.

sections.title: Forwarding Examples
sections.content:
FCoE packets can be forwarded in two modes depending on topology. In Dense mode, every switch along the path is an FCRB. The FCF at each switch takes a forwarding decision based on Fibre Channel addresses using the Fabric Shortest Path First (FSPF) routing protocol. The packet is then encapsulated in a TRILL header and sent to the next FCRB over a single TRILL hop. Each FCRB decapsulates the TRILL header, processes the FCoE packet at the FCF layer, and forwards it to the next hop.

In Sparse mode, not every switch along the path is an FCRB. An FCF at the entry switch makes an FSPF-based forwarding decision and encapsulates the packet in TRILL, allowing the underlying TRILL cloud to determine the path. The RBridge layer uses IS-IS routing to find the path to the egress RBridge.

FCoE control traffic, such as the FCoE Initialization Protocol (FIP), uses dedicated Ethernet frame types. FIP frames travel as multicast traffic, and each FCRB forwards a copy to its FCF entity as well as forwarding the packet through the TRILL network, ensuring all FCFs receive the initialization messages.
sections.eli5: Packets can take different paths. Dense mode: every switch is both a storage and data forwarder, deciding at each hop. Sparse mode: the first switch decides, then TRILL finds the path. Control messages make sure all forwarders know what's happening.

sections.title: Interoperability and Status
sections.content:
Security in FCoE over TRILL is handled by the underlying TRILL and FCoE protocols. TRILL has its own security considerations, and Fibre Channel includes security mechanisms in its specification. This document adds no new security implications beyond what those protocols provide.

RFC 6847 is informational and does not specify new protocols or require implementations to change. It describes an architecture that integrates two existing standards. The document does not introduce incompatibilities and has not been obsoleted.
sections.eli5: Security comes from the underlying Fibre Channel and TRILL protocols. This document just shows how to combine them without breaking anything.
